opus-5.5.text:
I think about it on two levels.

The first is breadth across tasks. For me, the real test of an "ultimate" model isn't whether it tops a benchmark in coding, math, or writing. It's whether it can walk into a domain it has never been trained on and get up to speed the way a smart person would. Give a good engineer a week with an unfamiliar codebase, or a good researcher a month in a neighboring field, and they become productive. That ability to adapt is what I'd call generalization. A model that is excellent across a thousand fixed tasks but brittle on the thousand-and-first is still, to me, a very sophisticated lookup table.

The second level is breadth across modalities and environments. Language turned out to be a surprisingly good compression of human knowledge, which is why text-only models went so far. But a lot of the world isn't written down: physical intuition, spatial reasoning, how to act in a messy environment where your actions change what you observe next. I think the ultimate model has to generalize across seeing, reading, acting, and getting feedback from the world, and not treat these as separate skills glued together.

That said, I'm a bit wary of the word "ultimate." In practice there's always a trade-off between generality and cost. You probably don't want your most general model running every small task, the same way you don't hire a Nobel laureate to sort the mail. So my working picture is a very general core, one that can learn, reason, and transfer, surrounded by efficient specialized pieces it knows how to call on or even create.

If I had to put it in one sentence, the goal isn't a model that already knows everything. It's a model that learns almost anything efficiently, and knows the limits of what it currently knows. That second part, calibration about its own ignorance, is underrated. A model that generalizes broadly but can't tell when it's out of its depth is more dangerous than one with narrower skills and honest uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
Chen Xie: That's a good question to start with, because I think "ultimate" is doing a lot of work in it. My honest view is that generalization isn't one axis. There's generalization across tasks, across modalities, across time, and across the actual physical world. People usually mean the first one when they talk about AGI, and I think that's the least interesting one.

Here's what I mean. If you train a model on enough text, it will generalize across language tasks surprisingly well. We've seen that. Summarization, translation, writing code, answering medical questions. That felt magical in 2022 and now it feels almost mundane. But that kind of generalization is still happening inside a very narrow envelope, which is the envelope of things humans have already written down.

The harder question is whether a model can generalize to situations where the training distribution simply doesn't cover the answer. A new disease. A robot in a kitchen it's never seen. A negotiation with people whose incentives aren't in any dataset. That's where I think an ultimate model has to go, and I don't think we get there just by scaling the current recipe. You need something closer to what a scientist does, which is form a hypothesis, test it against reality, and update when reality disagrees with you.

So to answer your question directly, I think an ultimate model should generalize about as broadly as a thoughtful human expert who's willing to admit ignorance. Not omniscient. Not able to answer everything on the first try. But able to walk into a domain it hasn't seen, figure out what it doesn't know, and acquire that knowledge efficiently. Breadth without that self-awareness is actually dangerous, because you get confident answers in places where confidence isn't earned.

And I'd add one thing that I think the field underweights. Generalization should also mean knowing when not to generalize. A lot of the failure modes we see today come from a model pattern-matching to something familiar when the situation is actually different. The ultimate model, to me, is one whose generalization is calibrated, not just wide.

astra-6.text:
I think an ultimate AI model should generalize broadly enough to handle unfamiliar problems, rather than just familiar tasks phrased differently. It should be able to take something it learned in one domain and apply it in another, recognize when that analogy breaks down, and learn from new evidence.

But breadth alone isn’t enough. A model can sound knowledgeable about everything and still be unreliable. What matters is whether it knows when it has enough information to act and when it needs to ask a question or test an assumption. So I’d want broad generalization paired with a very clear sense of its own limits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an ultimate AI model should generalize across tasks, domains, and environments—including situations that weren’t anticipated during training. It should be able to take something it learns in one area and use it meaningfully in another, rather than needing a separate training process for every new problem.

But breadth alone isn’t enough. It also needs to recognize when its knowledge doesn’t apply, ask for clarification, and learn from feedback. To me, the strongest form of generalization is being able to approach an unfamiliar problem, work out what matters, and adapt without pretending to know more than you do.
